analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income tax and IRS with a 15 percent national sales tax on nearly everything consumers buy.
analysis.headline: The National Retail Sales Tax Act of 1997 was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 1997 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, estate tax, and gift tax, abolish the IRS, and instead put a 15 percent tax on almost everything consumers buy in the United States. Businesses would buy everything tax-free, and low-income families would get a rebate covering sales tax up to the federal poverty line, paid through paychecks. States that set up matching sales taxes would collect the federal tax for a 1 percent fee, and the IRS would be shut down after fiscal year 2001.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and the wealthiest families gain the most: their income tax bills disappear entirely, the estate and gift tax is repealed, and because they save rather than spend much of their income, most of their economic life escapes taxation. Businesses gain from tax-free purchases of all business inputs, compensation for collecting the tax, and a credit for half the cost of new compliance equipment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, wealthy estates, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, estate tax, gift tax, and several excise taxes, eliminating income tax liability entirely for the highest earners and largest estates.
Exempts every purchase made for a business purpose in an active trade or business, so firms buy labor inputs, equipment, and inventory tax-free.

Pays registered businesses an administration credit of the greater of $200 or 0.5 percent of tax remitted (capped at 20 percent of tax due) and a credit for 50 percent of the cost of new compliance equipment.
Ends all appropriations for the Internal Revenue Service after fiscal year 2001 and moves payroll tax collection to the Social Security Administration.

analysis.who_pays: Working and middle-class families who spend nearly all of their income would pay a new 15 percent federal tax stacked on top of existing state sales taxes on almost everything they buy. The rebate offsets the tax only up to the poverty line, so families earning above poverty would pay substantially more tax on consumption than they ever owed under the progressive income tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Families who spend most of their income

drawbacks.text: The 15 percent tax applies to nearly all consumer purchases, including rent on real property and financial service fees, on top of existing state sales taxes, raising the effective price of everything a family buys.

The family consumption refund is capped at the tax on poverty-level spending, so a working family earning above poverty gets no full offset and pays more in sales tax than low- and moderate-income families would under a progressive income tax.
Government units and not-for-profit organizations would have to pay the tax on their purchases, raising the cost of public services and charity operations.
The bill requires a supermajority in the House and Senate to raise the tax rate, locking in the new structure even if it proves to fall too heavily on ordinary families.
By repealing the estate tax and ending income taxation of savings and capital, the bill shifts the overall tax burden away from the wealthiest households toward consumption by everyone else.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does simplify taxes and would end the income tax filing burden, and the poverty-level rebate protects the poorest families. But the core trade is replacing a progressive income tax with a flat consumption tax, which means the families who spend most of what they earn — most working households — would pay more, while high earners and inherited wealth pay far less. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the rebate cutoff means many working families above poverty lose.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee never took the bill up after referring it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Schaefer of Colorado introduced the bill on April 15, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Ten members cosponsored the bill: nine Republicans and one Democrat, Rep. Ralph Hall of Texas.
The action record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote — the bill sat in committee until the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyday taxpayers kept the existing progressive income tax code. The bill's biggest prospective winners — high earners, large estates, and businesses that would have bought everything tax-free — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday taxpayers kept the existing tax code

sides.party_line_note: All but one of the 11 sponsors were Republicans (nine of ten cosponsors were Republicans, with Rep. Ralph Hall of Texas the lone Democrat), and there were no floor votes to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill repeals the income, estate, and gift taxes and taxes only consumption, so households that save most of their income — overwhelmingly the wealthiest — would see their tax bills fall to nearly zero while everyone else pays 15 percent on spending. The gain at the top is paid for by the tax burden shifted onto working families' purchases.

Businesses would have to collect and remit the tax and keep records, but all business purchases are exempt and they receive an administration credit of up to 20 percent of tax remitted plus a credit for half the cost of new compliance equipment, so the collection burden is compensated.
Repealing the income tax and abolishing the IRS would eliminate most demand for income tax preparation and representation services. What the industry loses, ordinary filers would gain in simplicity.

The bill taxes explicitly charged fees (brokerage, loan origination, fund management) and imputed charges on interest-bearing accounts and debt, though the first $10,000 of financial intermediation receipts per year is exempt. Banks and funds would bear new tax on services they currently provide untaxed.

States with conforming sales taxes would become the permanent collectors of the federal tax, keeping a 1 percent administration fee. This locks in a federal role for state tax bureaucracies in exchange for revenue.
